questions.question: What is the practical purpose of `<React.Fragment>` (or `<>...</>`)?
options: It lets a component return several sibling elements without adding an extra DOM node
It memoizes the children so they never re-render
It creates a separate DOM tree isolated from the page
It defers rendering of children until the browser is idle
questions.explanation: A component must return a single root. A fragment groups siblings without producing a wrapper `div`, which keeps the DOM clean and avoids breaking layouts such as table rows or flex children.

questions.question: A button is written as `<button onClick={save()}>Save</button>`. What is the bug?
options: Handlers must be strings in JSX
`save()` runs during render and its return value is passed as the handler; it should be `onClick={save}` or `onClick={() => save()}`
`onClick` is not a valid prop on a `button`
Nothing; React defers the call until the click
questions.explanation: Parentheses invoke the function immediately while rendering. React needs a function reference to call later. Wrapping in an arrow function is needed only when you must pass arguments.

questions.question: With `items = []`, what does `{items.length && <List items={items} />}` render?
options: Nothing at all
An empty `List`
The text `0`
It throws an error
questions.explanation: `0 && x` evaluates to `0`, and React renders the number 0 as text (unlike `false`, `null` or `undefined`). Use `items.length > 0 && ...` or a ternary.

questions.question: What does JSX like `<Card title="Hi" />` compile to?
options: A real DOM node created with `document.createElement`
A string of HTML that is injected with `innerHTML`
A class instance of `Card` created immediately
A call to a JSX factory (`jsx()` / `React.createElement`) that returns a plain object describing the element
questions.explanation: JSX is syntax sugar. The compiled calls produce lightweight element objects; React later reconciles them against the previous tree and updates the real DOM as needed.

questions.question: What does 'lifting state up' mean in React, and when would you do it?
questions.model_answer: When two or more components need the same piece of changing data, move that state to their closest common ancestor and pass the value down as props, along with callbacks the children use to request changes. This keeps one source of truth and avoids copies drifting apart. For example, two filter widgets and a results list all depend on a `query` value, so the parent owns `query`. The trade-off is more prop passing; if the chain gets long, consider context or a store, but do not lift state higher than necessary because it widens re-renders.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want to hear 'single source of truth', 'closest common ancestor' and awareness that over-lifting causes needless re-renders and prop drilling.

questions.question: Changing `ref.current` of a `useRef` value inside an event handler does what?
options: Updates the value without scheduling a re-render
Triggers a re-render of the component
Resets the ref to its initial value on the next render
Throws because refs are read-only
questions.explanation: Refs are mutable boxes whose identity is stable across renders. Writing to `.current` is not tracked by React, so it never re-renders. Use refs for DOM nodes, timers and other values the UI does not display directly.

questions.question: A component runs `useEffect(() => { const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [])`. The counter stops at 1. Why?
options: `setInterval` cannot be used inside effects
The interval callback closes over the `count` from the first render, so it always sets 1; use `setCount(c => c + 1)`
The cleanup function clears the interval after one second
React batches updates so only the first is applied
questions.explanation: With an empty dependency array the effect captures the initial `count` (0) forever (a stale closure). A functional update reads the latest state, so no dependency is needed.

questions.question: In development with `<StrictMode>` (React 18), why does a mount-only `useEffect` appear to run twice?
options: It is a bug in React 18 that only affects development
The component is rendered on both server and client
React deliberately mounts, unmounts and remounts components to expose effects that are not cleaned up properly
Effects always run twice when the dependency array is empty
questions.explanation: Strict Mode simulates a remount to verify that setup and cleanup are symmetric. It does not happen in production builds. If double running breaks your code, the effect lacks proper cleanup.

questions.question: When does `useCallback(fn, deps)` actually improve performance?
options: Always, because it makes the function itself run faster
When the function is used only inside the same component's JSX
It prevents the component from re-rendering when state changes
When the stable function identity is passed to a memoized child or used as a dependency, so downstream work is skipped
questions.explanation: `useCallback` only preserves a reference. The benefit comes when something compares that reference (`React.memo`, another hook's deps). Otherwise it adds overhead for no gain.

questions.question: What are error boundaries in React and what do they not catch?
questions.model_answer: An error boundary is a class component (or a library wrapper such as `react-error-boundary`) implementing `getDerivedStateFromError` and/or `componentDidCatch`. It catches errors thrown while rendering, in lifecycle methods and in constructors of its descendants, and shows a fallback UI instead of unmounting the whole app. It does not catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code like `setTimeout` or promises, server-side rendering, or errors in the boundary itself. For those you use try/catch or `.catch`. In practice I place boundaries around independent regions (a widget, a route) and report the error to a monitoring service.
questions.explanation: Look for the correct list of exclusions and a sensible placement strategy rather than one global boundary.

questions.question: What makes a good custom hook, and how would you test one?
questions.model_answer: A custom hook extracts reusable stateful logic (not UI), named `useX`, with a small, stable API, such as `useDebouncedValue(value, delay)` or `useLocalStorage(key)`. It composes built-in hooks, cleans up its own effects and does not hide unrelated concerns. Each call has isolated state, so sharing the hook does not share data. To test, render it with `renderHook` from React Testing Library, drive it with `act`, use fake timers for time-based behavior and assert on the returned values. For logic with network access I mock the fetch layer instead of the hook.
questions.explanation: Strong answers distinguish sharing logic from sharing state and mention cleanup plus realistic testing tools.

questions.question: Which statement about `useLayoutEffect` versus `useEffect` is correct?
options: `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after DOM mutations and before the browser paints, so it suits measuring layout but can block painting
`useLayoutEffect` runs before the render function executes
`useEffect` always runs before the DOM is updated
`useLayoutEffect` is the recommended default because it is faster
questions.explanation: `useEffect` is deferred until after paint, while `useLayoutEffect` blocks paint so you can read layout and synchronously re-render without flicker. Overusing it hurts responsiveness, and it warns during server rendering.

questions.question: A list of rows with text inputs uses the array index as `key`. The user types in row 2, then another row is inserted at the top. What happens?
options: Nothing, because React diffs by value rather than key
Inputs keep their typed text by position, so the text appears in the wrong logical row
All inputs are cleared since the keys changed
React throws a duplicate-key warning and stops rendering
questions.explanation: State and DOM nodes are tied to the key. With index keys, inserting at the top shifts items but the key-to-instance mapping stays positional, so instance state is attached to the wrong data. Use stable ids.

questions.question: Explain React Server Components and how they differ from client components and traditional SSR.
questions.model_answer: Server Components render only on the server (at request or build time) and send a serialized description of the UI to the client; their code and dependencies are never shipped in the JS bundle. They can read databases or files directly and be async. Client Components (marked `'use client'`) are bundled, hydrate and can use state, effects and browser APIs. Traditional SSR renders HTML on the server but still ships and hydrates every component's JS. With RSC you keep heavy libraries on the server, reduce bundle size and avoid client waterfalls, while interactive parts stay client-side. Props passed from server to client must be serializable, and you pass server components to client ones as children.
questions.explanation: Candidates should separate 'SSR (HTML for first paint)' from 'RSC (zero client JS for those components)' and mention serialization limits.

questions.question: Context re-renders every consumer when its value changes. How do you structure context to avoid performance problems?
questions.model_answer: Split contexts by update frequency and concern (for example, separate state and dispatch, or theme versus user). Memoize the provider value with `useMemo` so a parent re-render does not create a new object each time. Keep rapidly changing data out of context or use a selector-based store (Zustand, Redux, `useSyncExternalStore`) so components subscribe to slices. Push providers down to the smallest subtree that needs them and wrap expensive consumers in `React.memo` with narrowed props. Measure with the React Profiler first, since most apps do not need these optimizations.
questions.explanation: Good answers combine splitting, memoized values and selector-based subscriptions, and are driven by measurement.

questions.question: What problem does `useSyncExternalStore` solve that a naive `useEffect` plus `useState` subscription does not?
options: It makes external stores deeply immutable
It batches every network request made by the store
It prevents tearing: during concurrent rendering all components read a consistent snapshot of an external store, and it works with SSR via a server snapshot
It removes the need for stores to notify subscribers
questions.explanation: With concurrent rendering, a render can be interrupted, so different components might read different values of a mutable external store. `useSyncExternalStore` forces synchronous consistent reads and provides `getServerSnapshot` for hydration. State libraries use it internally.

questions.question: A server-rendered React page logs hydration mismatch warnings and sometimes flashes wrong content. How do you find and fix the causes?
questions.model_answer: Hydration expects the first client render to produce the same markup the server sent. Typical causes: using `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` or locale-dependent formatting during render; reading `window`, `localStorage` or viewport size to decide what to render; invalid HTML nesting (a `div` in a `p`) that the browser repairs; and browser extensions altering the DOM. Fixes: render deterministic output first and apply client-only values in `useEffect` (or a `useSyncExternalStore` with a server snapshot), pass timestamps and locale from the server, use `useId` for generated ids, validate the markup, and use `suppressHydrationWarning` only for unavoidable leaf text like timestamps. I reproduce it by diffing the server HTML with the client DOM and check the dev warning's component stack.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want a systematic cause list and the 'render same thing twice, then enhance' principle.

questions.question: Design the data-fetching layer of a large React app that must stay responsive: caching, loading states, race conditions and optimistic updates.
questions.model_answer: Use a server-state library (React Query, SWR or Relay) rather than raw effects: queries are keyed, cached, deduplicated and refetched with stale-while-revalidate, which also solves out-of-order responses because only the latest key's result is applied. Combine with Suspense and error boundaries for declarative loading and failure states, and `startTransition` or `useDeferredValue` so navigation keeps the old UI interactive while new data loads. For mutations, apply optimistic updates to the cache, roll back on error from a saved snapshot, then invalidate affected keys. Prefetch on route intent (hover, router loaders), set staleTime per data type, and normalize only where entity sharing demands it. Keep client UI state separate (local state or a small store) from server state, and add abort signals for cancelled requests.
questions.explanation: Look for separation of server state vs UI state, race-condition handling, optimistic rollback and use of concurrent features.

questions.question: In `package.json`, what is the difference between `dependencies` and `devDependencies`?
options: `dependencies` install globally and `devDependencies` locally
`devDependencies` are optional and are never installed
`dependencies` are for the frontend and `devDependencies` for the backend
`dependencies` are needed at runtime in production; `devDependencies` are only for development tasks like testing, linting and building
questions.explanation: Production installs (`npm install --omit=dev`) skip dev dependencies, so a package your server imports at runtime must be in `dependencies`.

questions.question: What type is `process.env.PORT` when the variable is set to `3000`?
options: String
Number
Boolean
It depends on the shell
questions.explanation: All environment variables are strings. Convert explicitly, for example `Number(process.env.PORT) || 3000`, and remember that `'false'` is a truthy string.

questions.question: In Express, what happens if a middleware neither sends a response nor calls `next()`?
options: Express automatically calls the next middleware
The request hangs until the client times out
Express responds with a 404
The server process crashes
questions.explanation: Middleware must either end the cycle (`res.send`, `res.end`) or hand control onward with `next()`. Otherwise the connection stays open.

questions.question: What is `package-lock.json` for, and should you commit it?
questions.model_answer: `package-lock.json` records the exact resolved version tree (and integrity hashes) of every dependency, including transitive ones. Committing it makes installs reproducible across developers and CI, speeds up installation and means a surprise upstream release cannot silently change what you ship. Use `npm ci` in CI to install strictly from the lock file. Libraries published to npm do not ship their lock file to consumers, but applications should always commit it.
questions.explanation: Candidates should mention reproducibility, `npm ci` and that semver ranges in package.json alone are not pinned.

questions.question: What happens when an `EventEmitter` emits an `'error'` event and no listener is registered for it?
options: It is silently ignored like any other event
It is logged and the process continues
The error is thrown, and if uncaught the process crashes
The event is queued until a listener is added
questions.explanation: `'error'` is special-cased. Without a listener, Node throws the error. Streams, sockets and servers are emitters, so always attach error handlers.

questions.question: In a CommonJS module you write `exports = { add }` at the end. What does another file get from `require()`?
options: The object with `add`
`undefined`
A thrown `TypeError`
An empty object, because reassigning `exports` breaks its link to `module.exports`
questions.explanation: `exports` is just a local reference to `module.exports`. Reassigning it changes the local variable only; `require` returns `module.exports`. Use `module.exports = { add }` or `exports.add = add`.

questions.question: You must fetch 5 independent resources and still want results for the successful ones if some fail. Which approach fits?
options: `Promise.allSettled`, which waits for all and reports each outcome
`Promise.all`, which returns partial results on failure
`Promise.race`, which collects all fulfilled values
A `for` loop with `await` and no error handling
questions.explanation: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any promise rejects and discards the others' values. `allSettled` always resolves with `{status, value|reason}` entries, so you can use the successful ones.

questions.question: What is `AsyncLocalStorage` (from `node:async_hooks`) commonly used for?
options: Persisting data to disk between restarts
Carrying per-request context such as a request id through async calls without passing it as an argument
Sharing memory between worker threads
Caching DB results across requests
questions.explanation: It keeps a store that follows the async execution chain, so loggers and DB layers can read the current request id or user. It is not shared between requests or threads.

questions.question: How do you implement graceful shutdown for a Node HTTP service running in Kubernetes?
questions.model_answer: Handle `SIGTERM` (and `SIGINT`). On signal, mark the service not ready (fail the readiness probe) so the load balancer stops sending traffic, call `server.close()` to stop accepting new connections while in-flight requests finish, close keep-alive sockets (or use `closeIdleConnections()`), then close DB pools, queues and flush logs. Add a hard timeout slightly below `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` after which you `process.exit(1)`. Set a `preStop` sleep if endpoint propagation lags. Test by sending SIGTERM under load and verifying zero failed requests.
questions.explanation: Look for readiness flip, connection draining, resource cleanup and a forced-exit timeout.

questions.question: List the measures you would apply to harden an Express API against common attacks.
questions.model_answer: Validate and sanitize all input with a schema library (zod/Joi) and reject unknown fields; use parameterized queries to prevent injection; set security headers with `helmet`; configure CORS to an explicit allow-list; rate-limit and slow down auth endpoints; hash passwords with argon2 or bcrypt; store tokens in httpOnly, secure, sameSite cookies and add CSRF protection when using cookies; limit body size; avoid leaking stack traces in production; keep dependencies audited (`npm audit`, lockfile) and run as non-root. Log security events and keep secrets in a secret manager, not in the repo.
questions.explanation: Good answers are layered (input, transport, auth, dependencies, ops) and name concrete tools.

questions.question: On Node 15 and later, what is the default behavior when a promise rejects and nothing handles it?
options: A warning is printed and execution continues
The rejection is ignored silently
The process emits `unhandledRejection` and, with no handler, exits with a non-zero code
It is converted to a resolved `undefined`
questions.explanation: Since Node 15 `--unhandled-rejections=throw` is the default, turning unhandled rejections into uncaught exceptions. Handle rejections, and treat a global handler as a last-resort logger before exiting.

questions.question: You must call an API for 10,000 ids. How do you do it in Node without overwhelming the API or your memory?
questions.model_answer: Do not fire all requests at once (`Promise.all` over 10,000 promises) and do not await them one at a time. Use a bounded-concurrency pool: a library like `p-limit`/`p-queue`, or a small worker loop where N workers pull from a shared iterator. Choose N from the API's rate limit and latency. Add retries with exponential backoff and jitter for 429/5xx, honor `Retry-After`, use `AbortSignal.timeout` per request, and process results as they arrive (write to a stream or DB in batches) instead of accumulating everything. Track failures separately so a rerun can resume. If the API supports batch endpoints, prefer them.
questions.explanation: Look for bounded concurrency, backoff with jitter, streaming results and resumability.

questions.question: Your Node API's p99 latency spikes periodically while CPU shows one core at 100%. How do you diagnose an event-loop block?
questions.model_answer: Suspect synchronous work on the main thread. Measure event loop delay with `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay` or tools like clinic.js (`doctor`, `flame`) and collect a CPU profile (`node --cpu-prof` or Chrome DevTools attach) during a spike. Flame graphs reveal long synchronous frames: huge `JSON.parse/stringify`, sync crypto or `fs` calls, catastrophic regex backtracking, or large array sorts. Fix by streaming or chunking, moving CPU work to `worker_threads` or a separate service, using async APIs, yielding in loops with `setImmediate`, and validating regexes (or using RE2). Add an event-loop-lag metric and alert so regressions show up early.
questions.explanation: Strong answers measure first (profile, loop delay), then map findings to specific remedies.

questions.question: Which Node.js operations use the libuv thread pool (size controlled by `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`)?
options: TCP and UDP socket I/O
`setTimeout` and `setInterval` callbacks
All `async` functions
File system calls, `dns.lookup`, `crypto.pbkdf2`/`scrypt`/`randomBytes` and zlib compression
questions.explanation: Network sockets use OS-level async I/O (epoll/kqueue/IOCP) and timers use the loop's timer heap, neither of which need the pool. The default pool has 4 threads, so many concurrent `fs` or pbkdf2 calls queue behind each other.

questions.question: Design a webhook ingestion service in Node that must not lose events or process one twice, even with provider retries and worker crashes.
questions.model_answer: Acknowledge fast: verify the signature (HMAC over the raw body, constant-time compare and timestamp tolerance), persist the raw event with its provider event id in a table with a unique constraint, then return 2xx immediately. A queue (SQS/Kafka/BullMQ) or a transactional outbox feeds workers, so the HTTP path stays quick. Idempotency: the unique event id (or an idempotency key per side effect) makes duplicates no-ops, and handlers are written to be safely repeatable because delivery is at-least-once. Workers ack only after the transaction commits, use visibility timeouts, retry with backoff and route poison messages to a dead-letter queue with alerting. Handle ordering by per-entity partitioning or versions, and provide a replay tool using the stored raw events. Exactly-once processing is effectively at-least-once plus idempotency.
questions.explanation: Key signals: signature verification on raw body, persist-then-ack, idempotency keys, DLQ and replay.

questions.question: What is the relationship between a Docker image and a container?
options: An image is a read-only template; a container is a running (or stopped) instance created from it
A container is a template and an image is its running instance
They are the same thing under two names
An image is a virtual machine and a container is a snapshot of it
questions.explanation: Images are layered, immutable filesystems plus metadata. `docker run` adds a thin writable layer and a process on top, producing a container. Many containers can share one image.

questions.question: In a Node.js Dockerfile, why is `COPY package*.json ./` followed by `RUN npm ci` placed before `COPY . .`?
options: Because `npm ci` cannot read source files
So the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the dependency files change, not on every source edit
To make the final image smaller by removing source code
Docker requires manifests to be copied first
questions.explanation: Docker caches layers in order and invalidates all layers after a changed one. Putting rarely changing steps first keeps rebuilds fast.

questions.question: A team pushes application code and the provider handles the OS, runtime and scaling (as with Heroku or Google App Engine). Which service model is this?
options: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Software as a Service (SaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Bare-metal hosting
questions.explanation: IaaS gives you virtual machines and networks to manage yourself, PaaS manages the runtime for your code, and SaaS delivers a finished application to end users.

questions.question: What problem does a Kubernetes `Service` solve?
options: It stores persistent data for Pods
It schedules Pods onto nodes
It builds container images from source
It gives a set of Pods a stable virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances across them, even as Pods are replaced
questions.explanation: Pod IPs change whenever Pods are recreated. A Service selects Pods by label and provides a stable endpoint for clients and other services.

questions.question: Describe the typical stages of a CI/CD pipeline and what each protects against.
questions.model_answer: On every push: checkout and install dependencies with caching, then fast checks (lint, type check, unit tests) to catch obvious defects early. Next build an immutable artifact such as a container image tagged with the commit SHA, then run integration tests and security scans (dependency audit, image scan, secret detection). The artifact is deployed to staging for smoke and end-to-end tests, then promoted to production, manually approved (continuous delivery) or automatically (continuous deployment), with health checks and automatic rollback. Each stage fails fast and gives developers quick feedback; building once and promoting the same artifact ensures what was tested is what ships.
questions.explanation: Look for fail-fast ordering, build-once-promote-everywhere and a rollback story.

questions.question: A Kubernetes container with `resources.limits.memory: 256Mi` allocates 400Mi. What happens?
options: The container is killed by the kernel OOM killer (status `OOMKilled`) and restarted per the restart policy
It is throttled to run slower but keeps running
The Pod is rescheduled to a node with more memory immediately
The limit is ignored if the node has free memory
questions.explanation: CPU limits throttle, but memory is incompressible: exceeding the limit gets the process killed. Requests drive scheduling; limits are enforced at runtime.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of a Docker multi-stage build?
options: It builds each stage in parallel on different machines
The final image contains only runtime artifacts, leaving compilers and build tools in earlier discarded stages
It encrypts the layers of the final image
It lets a container run several processes safely
questions.explanation: A build stage can install toolchains and compile; the last stage copies only the output (for example a binary or `dist/`) onto a slim base. Images are smaller, faster to pull and expose less attack surface.

questions.question: Why is a stateless service easier to scale horizontally than a stateful one?
options: Stateless services use less CPU per request
Stateless services never need a database
Any instance can serve any request, so you can add or remove instances behind a load balancer without moving session data
Load balancers only support stateless protocols
questions.explanation: If user data lives in a shared store (database, cache, object storage) rather than instance memory, instances are interchangeable and disposable, which enables autoscaling and rolling replacement.

questions.question: Design a deployment pipeline for a containerized microservice that supports fast, safe rollbacks.
questions.model_answer: Build one immutable image per commit, tagged with the SHA, and push it to a registry. Deployment is declarative (Helm or Kustomize manifests in Git, ideally GitOps with Argo CD or Flux) so the desired version is a commit and rollback is a revert. Release with a rolling or canary strategy, gated by readiness probes and automated analysis of error rate and latency; the controller aborts and reverts automatically if SLO thresholds break. Database changes use backward-compatible expand/contract migrations so old and new versions can coexist. Feature flags decouple deploy from release so a bad feature is disabled without redeploying. Keep the previous ReplicaSet or release available and rehearse rollback regularly.
questions.explanation: Strong answers tie rollback to immutability, declarative state, automated health gates and compatible schema changes.

questions.question: Explain SLIs, SLOs, SLAs and error budgets, and how an error budget changes engineering decisions.
questions.model_answer: An SLI is a measured indicator of service health, such as the fraction of requests that succeed under 300 ms. An SLO is the target for that indicator over a window (99.9% over 30 days). An SLA is the contractual promise to customers, usually looser than the internal SLO, with penalties. The error budget is the allowed unreliability, `1 - SLO` (about 43 minutes per 30 days at 99.9%). While budget remains, teams can ship features and take risks; when it is burning too fast or is exhausted, the team slows launches and prioritizes reliability work. This turns the product-versus-stability argument into a data-driven policy, and burn-rate alerts replace noisy threshold alerts.
questions.explanation: Interviewers look for correct definitions and the policy angle: budgets as a shared decision tool.

questions.question: A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler targets 70% CPU utilization but never scales, and `kubectl top` shows high CPU. What is the most likely cause?
options: HPAs only work on StatefulSets
The cluster autoscaler must be disabled first
The Service type must be `LoadBalancer`
The Pods have no CPU `requests`, so utilization percentage cannot be computed
questions.explanation: HPA utilization is current usage divided by the container's requested CPU. Without requests there is no denominator and the HPA reports unknown metrics. Also confirm metrics-server is installed.

questions.question: You deploy with rolling updates and a release renames a database column. Which approach avoids errors while old and new versions run together?
options: Use expand/contract: add the new column and write to both, migrate readers, then drop the old column in a later release
Rename the column in the same release and rely on fast rollout
Stop all traffic during the migration
Keep the old version running forever
questions.explanation: During a rolling deploy both versions hit the same schema. Backward-compatible steps (expand, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, contract) let either version work at every moment and keep rollbacks safe.

questions.question: Your cloud bill grew 40% in a quarter. How do you find the cause and cut costs without hurting reliability?
questions.model_answer: First get visibility: enforce tagging by team and service, use Cost Explorer or a FinOps tool to break spend down by service, account and usage type, and compare with traffic growth to find unit-cost changes. Typical findings: oversized or idle instances, unattached volumes and old snapshots, NAT gateway and cross-AZ data transfer, logging and metrics ingestion volume, and over-provisioned databases. Actions: right-size using utilization data, autoscale and schedule non-production environments off-hours, use Savings Plans or reserved capacity for steady baseline and spot for fault-tolerant jobs, add storage lifecycle policies, reduce log verbosity or retention. Set budgets with alerts and make owners accountable for their cost per request. Validate each change against SLOs.
questions.explanation: Looks for measurement before action, knowledge of hidden cost drivers (data transfer, logs), and guardrails.

questions.question: What does a Kubernetes `PodDisruptionBudget` protect against?
options: Pods crashing due to application bugs
Too many replicas of an app being voluntarily evicted at once, for example during a node drain or cluster upgrade
Nodes losing power unexpectedly
Excess CPU usage by noisy neighbours
questions.explanation: A PDB sets `minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable` for voluntary disruptions. The eviction API refuses evictions that would violate it, so upgrades proceed gradually. It does not guard against involuntary failures such as hardware loss.

questions.question: Design an active-active multi-region architecture for a user-facing API. What are the hard parts and trade-offs?
questions.model_answer: Route users to the nearest healthy region with latency-based or geo DNS (or anycast) plus health checks. Stateless services deploy identically in each region. The hard part is data: choose per dataset between a globally consistent store (Spanner, CockroachDB, DynamoDB global tables with conflict rules) and region-owned data with asynchronous replication and per-user home regions. Eventually consistent replication needs conflict resolution (last-writer-wins, CRDTs or ownership), and cross-region latency makes synchronous writes expensive. Use idempotent writes and queues that replicate events. Plan failover: automated health-based traffic shift, capacity headroom so one region can absorb another's load, and regular game-day failover tests. Cost doubles and operational complexity rises, so confirm the RTO/RPO targets actually justify it versus active-passive.
questions.explanation: Look for a clear data-consistency strategy, capacity planning for failover and honest cost/complexity trade-offs.

questions.question: Which command creates a new branch and switches to it in a single step?
options: `git branch feature-x --switch`
`git new feature-x`
`git switch -c feature-x`
`git checkout feature-x --create-only`
questions.explanation: `git switch -c name` (or the older `git checkout -b name`) creates the branch at the current commit and moves HEAD onto it. Plain `git branch name` creates it without switching.

questions.question: In Git, what does `HEAD` refer to?
options: The first commit of the repository
The newest commit on the remote
The staging area
The commit (usually via the current branch) that your working tree is based on
questions.explanation: HEAD normally points to a branch name, which points to a commit. In detached HEAD state it points directly at a commit.

questions.question: You staged `config.js` by mistake and want to unstage it but keep your edits. Which command does that?
options: `git restore --staged config.js`
`git restore config.js`
`git reset --hard config.js`
`git rm config.js`
questions.explanation: `git restore --staged` removes the file from the index only (older equivalent: `git reset HEAD file`). Plain `git restore file` discards the working-tree edits instead.

questions.question: What does `git cherry-pick <sha>` do?
options: Moves the original commit to the current branch without copying
Applies the changes of that commit onto the current branch as a new commit with a different hash
Merges the whole branch containing that commit
Deletes the commit from its original branch
questions.explanation: Cherry-pick replays a commit's diff, creating a new commit with a new id. The original stays where it was, so the same change can later conflict or duplicate on merge.

questions.question: Why is `git push --force-with-lease` preferred over `git push --force` after rebasing your own feature branch?
options: It is faster because it skips compression
It also rewrites the teammates' local copies automatically
It refuses to overwrite the remote branch if someone else pushed commits you have not seen
It only pushes a single commit
questions.explanation: `--force-with-lease` checks that the remote ref is still what you last fetched. A plain `--force` can silently destroy a colleague's newer work.

questions.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict, and what practices reduce how often they happen?
questions.model_answer: Run `git status` to see conflicted files, open each one and understand both sides of the `<<<<<<<` markers (use `git log` or `git blame` to see intent), edit to the correct combined result, remove markers, run tests, `git add` the files and finish with `git commit` (or `git rebase --continue`). A merge tool or `git checkout --ours/--theirs` helps for whole-file decisions, and `git merge --abort` returns to the start. To reduce conflicts: keep branches short-lived, merge or rebase from main often, make small focused PRs, avoid mass reformatting mixed with logic, agree on formatters, and communicate when touching shared files.
questions.explanation: A good answer is calm and systematic: understand intent, verify with tests, and prevent via small frequent integration.

questions.question: You are in detached HEAD state, make two commits, then run `git switch main`. What is the risk?
options: Git automatically merges them into main
Git refuses to switch until you commit
The commits are deleted immediately and cannot be recovered
The commits are no longer referenced by any branch, so they can be lost unless you create a branch or find them via reflog
questions.explanation: Commits made in detached HEAD are only reachable from HEAD. After switching away Git warns you; run `git branch rescue <sha>` (from the warning or `git reflog`) before garbage collection removes them.

questions.question: What does `git rebase --onto main featureA featureB` do?
options: Replays the commits that are in `featureB` but not in `featureA` onto `main`
Merges `featureA` and `featureB` into `main`
Renames `featureB` to `featureA`
Deletes `featureA` and rebases `main` onto `featureB`
questions.explanation: The three-argument form is `--onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch>`. It takes the commits after `upstream` up to `branch` and replays them on `newbase`. It is the standard way to move a branch that was built on top of another feature branch.

questions.question: Compare merge commits, squash merges and rebase-and-merge for pull requests. Which would you standardize on for a team and why?
questions.model_answer: Merge commits preserve full branch history and exact commit hashes but make the graph noisy and can contain 'fix typo' commits. Squash merges produce one commit per PR, giving a clean linear main where each commit is a reviewable, revertable unit; the downside is losing granular history and making stacked branches awkward. Rebase-and-merge keeps individual commits linearly but rewrites hashes, and it works only if commits are individually clean and tested. For most product teams I standardize on squash merge with a strong PR title convention, since it makes `git bisect` and reverts simple; for teams that curate atomic commits (like kernel-style work) rebase-and-merge fits. Whatever the choice, enforce it in repo settings, protect main and require CI.
questions.explanation: The answer matters less than reasoning about bisectability, revert-ability, history fidelity and team discipline.

questions.question: A repository has grown to 8 GB because binaries were committed over the years and clones take 20 minutes. How do you fix it and prevent a repeat?
questions.model_answer: Diagnose with `git count-objects -vH` and `git rev-list --objects --all` (or `git-sizer`) to find the largest blobs. Rewrite history to remove them using `git filter-repo` (not the slow legacy `filter-branch`), coordinate a freeze since all hashes change, force-push, and have everyone re-clone; pursue server-side cleanup and garbage collection. Move genuinely needed large assets to Git LFS or an artifact store and reference them by version. Mitigate clone cost for those who cannot wait using `--filter=blob:none` partial clones, shallow clones in CI and sparse checkout. Prevent regressions with a pre-receive hook or CI size check and `.gitignore` for build output. Communicate the plan, back up the original repo and archive old links, since open PRs and tags need migration.
questions.explanation: Expect knowledge of filter-repo, LFS, partial clone and the organizational cost of rewriting shared history.

questions.question: What is the difference between smoke testing and regression testing?
options: Smoke tests check performance, regression tests check security
Smoke tests quickly check that the most critical functions work after a build; regression tests verify that existing behavior has not broken after a change
Smoke testing is done only by customers
They are the same, just different names
questions.explanation: A smoke suite is a small, fast gate (does the app start, can users log in). Regression suites are broader and run to catch unintended side effects of changes.

questions.question: Which best describes black-box testing?
options: Testing every line of code using a debugger
Testing only the database layer
Testing behavior against requirements through inputs and outputs, without relying on knowledge of the internal code
Testing performed by the original developer only
questions.explanation: Black-box techniques (equivalence partitioning, boundary analysis) derive tests from the specification. White-box techniques use knowledge of code structure, for example to reach all branches.

questions.question: An input field accepts ages from 18 to 65 inclusive. Which set of values best applies boundary value analysis?
questions.explanation: Defects cluster at the edges. Test just outside and exactly on each boundary: 17 (invalid), 18 (valid), 65 (valid), 66 (invalid), plus optionally a mid value.

questions.question: What information should a high-quality bug report contain?
questions.model_answer: A clear, specific title; environment details (app version, OS, browser, device, account type); numbered steps to reproduce; expected versus actual result; frequency (always or intermittent); and evidence such as screenshots, video, logs, console errors or HAR files. Add severity and the user impact, and link related tickets. Keep one issue per report and avoid speculation about the cause unless supported by evidence. The goal is that a developer who has never seen the issue can reproduce it in minutes without asking follow-up questions.
questions.explanation: Interviewers value reproducibility, evidence and impact over long prose.

questions.question: Tests pass when run individually but some fail when the whole suite runs in random order. What is the most likely root cause?
options: Tests share state (database rows, globals, files) and depend on execution order
The assertion library has a bug
The test runner is running too fast
The tests are too short
questions.explanation: Order-dependent failures indicate leaked state or hidden coupling. Fix by giving each test its own setup/teardown, isolated data or transactions rolled back after each test, and never relying on another test's side effects.

questions.question: Given `if (a && b) { ... }`, how does branch coverage differ from line coverage?
options: Branch coverage counts only functions
Line coverage can reach 100% with one test where the condition is true, while branch coverage also requires a test where it is false
They are always identical
Line coverage includes conditions, branch coverage counts comments
questions.explanation: Branch coverage checks that each decision outcome was exercised. Neither metric proves assertions are meaningful; high coverage with weak assertions still misses bugs.

questions.question: In a browser end-to-end test, a button appears after an async request. Which approach is most reliable?
options: Add a fixed `sleep(5000)` before clicking
Retry the whole test three times
Wait explicitly for the element or condition (for example, an auto-waiting locator or `waitFor`)
Click repeatedly in a loop until no error
questions.explanation: Fixed sleeps are either too slow or too short and cause flakiness. Condition-based waits proceed as soon as the app is ready and fail clearly with a timeout.

questions.question: You inherit a legacy codebase with almost no tests. How do you start introducing automated testing without stalling feature work?
questions.model_answer: Start with characterization tests that lock in current behavior at the highest-value entry points (key API endpoints and critical user journeys), since unit-testing tangled code is hard. Add tests whenever you fix a bug or touch an area (the boy-scout rule), and use seams (dependency injection, extracting functions) to make code testable gradually. Set up CI with a fast runner first, then add a coverage baseline that cannot decrease for changed lines rather than a global target. Prioritize risk: payments, auth and data integrity before cosmetic code. Share quick wins and track escaped defects to show value to the team and management.
questions.explanation: Look for pragmatism: characterization tests, incremental coverage on changed code and risk-based priorities.

questions.question: During a load test you report 'average response time 180 ms' while some users complain of 8-second waits. What is the best way to report latency?
options: Report only the average, since it is the most stable
Report only the minimum response time
Discard the slowest 10% as noise
Report percentiles (p50, p95, p99) and the max, because averages hide long-tail outliers
questions.explanation: Latency distributions are skewed. Tail percentiles show what real users experience and often drive SLOs. Also watch for coordinated omission in test tools that pause when the system stalls.

questions.question: A function behaves differently depending on `Date.now()`. What is the best way to make its tests deterministic?
options: Inject a clock (or use fake timers) so the test controls the current time
Run the tests only at midnight
Assert with a very wide time tolerance and hope
Skip testing time-dependent logic
questions.explanation: Treat time like any other external dependency: pass it in or use a fake clock so you can test boundaries such as month ends, DST changes and expiry without waiting.

questions.question: Plan the performance testing for an e-commerce site expecting 10x traffic during a flash sale next month.
questions.model_answer: Define goals first: expected peak requests per second, concurrent users, and SLOs such as p95 under 500 ms with under 0.1% errors. Model realistic traffic from production analytics (browse-heavy mix with a checkout spike) using k6, Gatling or Locust, with production-like data volumes and environment sizing. Run baseline, load, stress (find the breaking point), spike and soak tests. Instrument everything (APM, DB metrics, queue depth) to find bottlenecks, typically database connections, hot rows for inventory, third-party payment limits and cache stampedes. Fix, retest and verify autoscaling and graceful degradation, such as a waiting room or disabled recommendations. Agree a rollback and runbook, do a final rehearsal and monitor live with alerts.
questions.explanation: Strong candidates start from goals and realistic workload models, then iterate with observability and plan degradation.

questions.question: You are asked to define the quality strategy for an organization with 50 engineering teams. What principles, ownership model and metrics do you set?
questions.model_answer: Make quality a team-owned engineering responsibility, with a small central enablement group providing frameworks, tooling and coaching rather than gatekeeping. Standardize the pyramid: many fast unit tests, contract tests between services, a thin layer of end-to-end tests on critical journeys, and production checks (synthetic monitoring, feature flags, canaries). Require CI gates for tests, security scanning and accessibility, with flaky-test quarantine and a budget for pipeline time. Measure outcomes rather than activity: change failure rate, mean time to restore, escaped defects by severity, lead time, flake rate and customer-reported issues; avoid vanity metrics like raw coverage. Review incidents blamelessly and feed lessons into shared checklists. Roll out by supporting a few pilot teams first, then scale what works.
questions.explanation: Look for DORA-style outcome metrics, shift-left plus shift-right, and an enablement (not gatekeeper) org model.

questions.question: Which task is an example of unsupervised learning?
options: Grouping customers into segments by purchasing behavior without predefined labels
Predicting house prices from labelled sales
Classifying emails as spam or not spam using labelled examples
Forecasting next month's sales from past labelled values
questions.explanation: Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data (clustering, dimensionality reduction). The other options all learn from known target values, which makes them supervised.

questions.question: What is the difference between a model parameter and a hyperparameter?
options: Parameters are set by hand; hyperparameters are learned
Parameters are learned from data during training; hyperparameters are set beforehand and control the learning process
Both are learned by gradient descent
Hyperparameters exist only in neural networks
questions.explanation: Weights and biases are parameters fitted by the optimizer. Learning rate, tree depth and regularization strength are hyperparameters chosen by you, usually tuned on a validation set.

questions.question: A `city` feature has values like Paris, Tokyo and Lima with no natural order. Why is one-hot encoding usually better than mapping them to 1, 2, 3 for a linear model?
options: One-hot encoding always reduces the number of features
Linear models cannot process integers
Integer codes imply a false ordering and distances between cities that the model would treat as meaningful
Integer codes use more memory
questions.explanation: For nominal categories, numeric codes inject arbitrary order. One-hot gives each category its own weight. Tree models are less sensitive, and high-cardinality features may need target or embedding encodings instead.

questions.question: During gradient descent training, the loss oscillates wildly or increases. What is the most likely issue?
options: The learning rate is too low
The dataset is too small to compute gradients
The model has too few parameters
The learning rate is too high, so updates overshoot the minimum
questions.explanation: Large steps jump across the valley of the loss surface and can diverge. Reduce the learning rate, use a schedule or an adaptive optimizer, and check feature scaling.

questions.question: Explain gradient descent to a non-expert, and say how stochastic and mini-batch variants differ.
questions.model_answer: Imagine standing on a foggy hill and wanting the lowest point: you feel the slope under your feet and take a step downhill, repeatedly. In training, the 'hill' is the loss, the slope is the gradient with respect to the model parameters, and the step size is the learning rate. Batch gradient descent computes the gradient over the whole dataset per step, which is accurate but slow. Stochastic gradient descent uses one example per step, which is fast and noisy; the noise can help escape poor minima. Mini-batch uses small groups (such as 32 to 512 examples), balancing efficient hardware use with reasonably stable gradients, and is the standard in deep learning.
questions.explanation: The intuition plus the trade-off between gradient accuracy, speed and noise is the target.

questions.question: Why does a random forest usually generalize better than a single deep decision tree?
options: Averaging many trees trained on bootstrapped samples and random feature subsets reduces variance
Each tree in the forest is shallower and therefore has higher bias
It trains on the test set as well
It removes the need for any hyperparameters
questions.explanation: Single deep trees overfit. Bagging with decorrelated trees averages out their individual errors, cutting variance without raising bias much. Out-of-bag samples also give a free validation estimate.

questions.question: What happens to dropout during inference in a standard framework?
options: Units are still dropped randomly with the same probability
Dropout is disabled and all units are used (activations are scaled consistently with training)
Only half of the network is used
Dropout is applied to the weights permanently
questions.explanation: Dropout is a training-time regularizer. With inverted dropout the scaling is applied during training, so at test time the full network runs deterministically (`model.eval()` in PyTorch).

questions.question: You use SMOTE oversampling to balance classes and then run K-fold cross-validation on the oversampled dataset. What is wrong?
options: SMOTE cannot be used with cross-validation in any form
Nothing; oversampling first is the standard approach
Synthetic samples derived from validation-fold neighbours leak into training, inflating scores; resampling must happen inside each training fold only
K-fold only works on balanced data
questions.explanation: Oversampling before splitting puts near-copies of the same points in both train and validation folds, so the evaluation is optimistic. Use a pipeline that resamples only the training portion of each fold.

questions.question: What does an ROC AUC of 0.85 mean for a binary classifier?
options: 85% of predictions are correct
The model has 85% precision at all thresholds
15% of positives are missed at every threshold
A randomly chosen positive example is ranked above a randomly chosen negative one with probability 0.85
questions.explanation: AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds and is independent of the chosen cutoff and class prior. It says nothing about calibration or the precision at a specific operating point.

questions.question: Compare L1 and L2 regularization. When would you use each, and what is elastic net?
questions.model_answer: Both add a penalty on weight size to the loss. L2 (ridge) penalizes squared weights, shrinks them smoothly toward zero and handles correlated features by sharing weight; it rarely gives exact zeros. L1 (lasso) penalizes absolute values, which drives some coefficients exactly to zero, giving sparse models and built-in feature selection, but it is unstable with highly correlated features (it picks one arbitrarily). Elastic net combines both penalties, giving sparsity while remaining stable for correlated groups. Choose L1 when you suspect few features matter or need interpretability, L2 as a default for predictive stability, elastic net for many correlated predictors, and tune the strength by cross-validation after scaling features.
questions.explanation: Look for the geometry intuition (sparsity vs shrinkage), correlated-feature behavior and the need to scale features.

questions.question: Why do Transformers use layer normalization instead of batch normalization?
options: Layer norm normalizes across features per example, so it does not depend on batch size or sequence padding statistics and works at inference with batch size 1
Layer norm is cheaper in every case
Batch norm cannot be applied to matrices
Layer norm removes the need for residual connections
questions.explanation: Batch norm relies on batch statistics, which are noisy for small batches and awkward for variable-length sequences. Layer norm computes mean and variance per token over the feature dimension, giving identical behavior in training and inference.

questions.question: A classifier outputs 0.8 for a group of cases, but only 55% of those cases are actually positive. Which property is lacking?
options: Recall
Calibration: predicted probabilities do not match observed frequencies
Statistical power
Stationarity
questions.explanation: A calibrated model's predicted probability reflects the true likelihood. A model can rank well (high AUC) while being miscalibrated. Fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data, and check reliability diagrams.

questions.question: For an LLM-powered product that must answer questions about a company's private documents, how do you choose between prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and fine-tuning?
questions.model_answer: Start with prompting and a strong baseline because it is cheapest to iterate. For knowledge that is private, large or changing, use RAG: chunk and embed documents, retrieve relevant passages (often hybrid keyword plus vector search with reranking), and put them in the prompt with citations. This keeps data fresh, auditable and permission-aware. Fine-tuning is for changing behavior, format or style, or distilling to a smaller cheaper model; it is a poor way to inject facts that change. Often combine them: fine-tune for tone and structure and RAG for facts. Evaluate with a labelled question set measuring retrieval recall, answer faithfulness and refusal behavior, and add guardrails such as access control at retrieval time and prompt-injection defenses.
questions.explanation: Strong answers match each technique to the problem (knowledge vs behavior) and include evaluation and security.

questions.question: Customer behavior changed after a pricing update, so the relationship between features and churn is different even though the feature distributions look the same. What is this called?
options: Covariate shift
Class imbalance
Concept drift (the conditional distribution P(y|x) changed)
Data leakage
questions.explanation: Covariate shift changes P(x) while P(y|x) stays fixed. Concept drift changes the mapping itself, so monitoring inputs alone will miss it. You need label-based monitoring, delayed performance metrics and scheduled or triggered retraining.

questions.question: Your recommender performs well offline but poorly online. How do you investigate training-serving skew, feedback loops and evaluation mismatch?
questions.model_answer: Start by checking for skew: log the exact features served at prediction time and compare their distributions and computation with the training pipeline; a feature store with a single definition for batch and online prevents drift in logic, time zones, null handling and freshness. Check leakage in offline evaluation (random split on time-ordered data, features computed with future information) and use time-based splits. Offline metrics like AUC may not align with online goals, so validate with interleaving or A/B tests and counterfactual estimators (inverse propensity scoring) because logged data is biased by the previous policy. Feedback loops cause popularity bias and shrinking exploration, so add exploration (epsilon or Thompson sampling) and measure diversity and long-term retention. Also examine latency-driven fallbacks, cold start, and cache staleness in production.
questions.explanation: Looks for training-serving skew, leakage, proper online evaluation and awareness of selection bias in logged data.

questions.question: What does a large standard deviation tell you about a dataset?
options: Values are all close to the mean
The mean equals the median
The dataset has no outliers
Values are widely spread around the mean
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean. It is in the same unit as the data, and it is sensitive to outliers.

questions.question: In pandas, `orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")` returns which rows?
options: All rows from `orders`, with customer columns filled with NaN where no match exists
Only rows that appear in both tables
All rows from `customers` only
Only unmatched rows
questions.explanation: A left join keeps every row of the left table. Unmatched right-side columns become NaN. An inner join would drop orders without matching customers.

questions.question: Which chart is most appropriate for examining the distribution of a single continuous variable such as order value?
options: A pie chart
A histogram
A line chart over categories
A stacked bar chart
questions.explanation: Histograms bin a continuous variable to show shape, skew, spread and outliers. Pie charts compare parts of a whole and line charts show order or time.

questions.question: You receive a new CSV dataset. Walk through your first steps of exploratory data analysis.
questions.model_answer: First clarify the business question and what each column means, then load the data and check shape, types, and a sample of rows. Look at missing values per column, duplicates, and impossible values (negative ages, future dates). Summarize numeric columns (mean, median, quartiles, min and max) and plot histograms and boxplots; profile categorical columns by counts and cardinality. Examine relationships with the target through group statistics, scatter plots and a correlation matrix, and check time trends and seasonality if there is a date. Note data quality problems and assumptions, validate against known totals from the source system, and document findings and next cleaning steps before modeling.
questions.explanation: A systematic approach that starts with understanding and validation, not jumping straight to a model.

questions.question: In hypothesis testing, what is a Type II error?
options: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true
Choosing the wrong test statistic
Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false (a missed real effect)
Calculating the p-value incorrectly
questions.explanation: Type I is a false positive (probability alpha). Type II is a false negative (probability beta); power equals `1 - beta`. Larger samples and larger effects increase power.

questions.question: What does the Central Limit Theorem say?
options: Every dataset becomes normal if you collect enough rows
The sample mean always equals the population mean
Medians are always normally distributed
The distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as sample size grows, even if the population is not normal (given finite variance)
questions.explanation: The CLT justifies using normal-based confidence intervals and tests for means with reasonably large samples. It concerns the sampling distribution of the mean, not the raw data, and convergence is slower for heavy-tailed distributions.

questions.question: You test 20 independent metrics at alpha = 0.05 and one shows p = 0.03. If all 20 null hypotheses are true, what is the approximate probability of at least one false positive?
options: About 64%
About 5%
About 20%
About 1%
questions.explanation: `1 - 0.95^20` is roughly 0.64. This is the multiple comparisons problem; control it by pre-registering a primary metric or adjusting with Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg.

questions.question: You are building a churn prediction model for a subscription product. What features would you engineer and what pitfalls would you avoid?
questions.model_answer: Define churn precisely (for example no activity or cancellation within 30 days) and fix a prediction time. Engineer features computed only from data before that time: recency, frequency and monetary-style usage counts over several windows (7, 30, 90 days), trends such as week-over-week change, tenure, plan and price, support tickets, payment failures, feature adoption and engagement diversity. Encode categories sensibly and handle missing values consistently. Pitfalls: label leakage (using cancellation-related events recorded after the cutoff), random splits on time-ordered data instead of time-based splits, ignoring class imbalance, and building a model without an action plan. Evaluate with precision at top-K and uplift, not just AUC, and monitor for drift.
questions.explanation: The key signal is time-aware feature construction with no leakage and a link to the business action.

questions.question: To detect an effect half as large with the same power and significance level in an A/B test, how does the required sample size per group change?
options: It roughly doubles
It increases roughly four times
It stays the same
It halves
questions.explanation: Sample size scales with `1 / effect^2` (for a fixed variance). Halving the minimum detectable effect therefore needs about four times as many users, which is why small lifts are costly to detect.

questions.question: An A/B test designed for a 50/50 split shows 52,000 users in control and 48,000 in treatment. What does this indicate?
options: The treatment is performing worse, so users left
It is an expected random fluctuation
A likely sample ratio mismatch, pointing to an assignment or logging bug that makes results untrustworthy
The test has reached statistical significance
questions.explanation: With 100,000 users a 50/50 split should be within a fraction of a percent, so a 4% gap is highly improbable by chance. Run a chi-square test, investigate bot filtering, redirects and exposure logging before trusting any metric.

questions.question: A product team shipped a feature to all users and now asks whether it increased retention. No experiment was run. How would you estimate its causal effect?
questions.model_answer: Be upfront that observational estimates need assumptions. If the rollout was staggered by region or time, use difference-in-differences with parallel-trends checks or synthetic control built from similar untreated units. If adoption was optional, compare adopters and non-adopters only after adjusting for confounders via matching or propensity-score weighting, and be aware that engaged users self-select. If an arbitrary cutoff or an instrument exists (eligibility threshold, a random outage), regression discontinuity or instrumental variables can help. Run placebo tests on pre-period data and sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding, report uncertainty ranges rather than a single number, and recommend a holdout group for future launches.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want honest framing of assumptions, an appropriate method for the data situation, and validation checks.

questions.question: Your A/B test on revenue per user is underpowered because the metric is extremely skewed and noisy. What options do you have to reach a decision faster without cheating?
questions.model_answer: Reduce variance: use CUPED, regressing out pre-experiment behavior of each user, which often cuts variance by 20 to 50%. Winsorize or cap extreme values with the cap decided in advance, or use a more sensitive proxy metric (conversion rate, add-to-cart) validated against revenue historically. Use stratified or paired designs and increase exposure to more traffic. Use sequential testing methods (always-valid p-values, group sequential boundaries) when peeking is required rather than repeated naive looks. Bootstrap confidence intervals for the ratio. Pre-register the primary metric and stopping rule, and report that a longer test or accepting a bigger minimum detectable effect is the honest alternative when these are not enough.
questions.explanation: Look for CUPED, pre-specified capping, sequential testing and discipline about not p-hacking.

questions.question: In Flutter, when should a widget be a `StatefulWidget` instead of a `StatelessWidget`?
options: When it contains more than one child widget
When it uses images
When it is placed inside a `Scaffold`
When the widget holds data that changes over its lifetime and the UI must rebuild in response
questions.explanation: Stateless widgets describe UI purely from their constructor arguments. Stateful widgets own a `State` object, mutated with `setState`, that triggers a rebuild.

questions.question: Why do Android and iOS layouts use density-independent units (dp/sp on Android, points on iOS)?
options: So UI elements appear at a consistent physical size across screens with different pixel densities
To make apps run faster on older devices
To avoid using layout constraints
Because pixels are not supported by the OS
questions.explanation: Devices have vastly different pixels per inch. Density-independent units are scaled by the system, and `sp` additionally respects the user's font size setting for accessibility.

questions.question: What is the purpose of deep links (Android App Links / iOS Universal Links)?
options: To encrypt traffic between the app and server
To open a specific screen in the app directly from a URL, falling back to the website if the app is not installed
To install updates silently
To let apps read each other's local storage
questions.explanation: Verified links tie your domain to your app so tapping an https link opens the right content in-app. They power marketing campaigns, notifications and sharing and require a hosted association file on your domain.

questions.question: Which Android API is designed for deferrable background work that must eventually run even if the app is closed or the device restarts?
options: A plain `Thread` started in `onCreate`
`AsyncTask`
WorkManager
A foreground `Activity` timer
questions.explanation: WorkManager persists work requests and respects constraints such as network and charging, handling Doze and app restarts. Plain threads die with the process, and `AsyncTask` is deprecated.

questions.question: Several simultaneous API calls get HTTP 401 because the access token expired. What is the best way to handle refresh?
options: Let every call refresh the token independently
Log the user out immediately
Increase the token lifetime to a year
Use a single in-flight refresh request that other calls wait for, then retry them with the new token
questions.explanation: Concurrent refreshes can race and invalidate each other, especially with rotating refresh tokens. A shared promise or mutex in the HTTP interceptor refreshes once, then replays queued requests.

questions.question: How do you handle app versioning, forced upgrades and API backward compatibility for a mobile app, given users update slowly?
questions.model_answer: Treat the API as a long-lived contract: version it or evolve it additively (new optional fields, never removing or repurposing existing ones) because old app versions remain in the wild for months. The app sends its version and platform in headers, and the backend can return a minimum supported version so the client shows a soft prompt or a blocking update screen for critical security or breaking changes. Use remote config and feature flags to disable broken features server-side without a store release, and staged rollouts (Play Console, phased release on iOS) to catch crashes early. Maintain a support matrix and analytics of version adoption to decide when to retire an API version, with a deprecation timeline.
questions.explanation: Look for additive API evolution, minimum-version checks, flags and staged rollout.

questions.question: At 60 fps, roughly how much time does the UI thread have to produce each frame?
options: About 16 ms
About 160 ms
About 1 ms
About 100 ms
questions.explanation: 1000 ms divided by 60 is about 16.7 ms. Any main-thread work longer than that (parsing JSON, image decoding, heavy layout) causes dropped frames and visible jank.

questions.question: An Android app keeps state only in a `ViewModel`. After the user leaves the app for hours, the system kills the process and the user returns to a blank form. Why, and what is the fix?
options: ViewModels are cleared on rotation, so use a static variable
ViewModels do not survive process death; persist small UI state with `SavedStateHandle` or `onSaveInstanceState`, and durable data in a database
The OS never kills processes, so this is a bug in the form
Use a larger heap with `largeHeap=true`
questions.explanation: A ViewModel survives configuration changes like rotation but lives in the process memory. When the process is killed, the system only restores what you saved in the saved-state bundle. Test with 'Don't keep activities' and `adb shell am kill`.

questions.question: How would you monitor and reduce the crash rate of a production mobile app?
questions.model_answer: Integrate a crash reporter (Firebase Crashlytics or Sentry) with symbolication/dSYM and ProGuard/R8 mapping uploads so stack traces are readable, plus breadcrumbs, app version, device and OS tags. Track crash-free sessions and users per release, and alert when a new release regresses. Triage by impact and frequency, reproduce on the affected devices or OS versions, and fix top crash clusters first, often null handling, threading and out-of-memory problems. Use staged rollouts and kill-switch feature flags to limit blast radius, add ANR and startup monitoring, and add tests plus lint rules for recurring causes. Close the loop by checking that the fix actually dropped the crash signature in the next release.
questions.explanation: Signals: readable stack traces, per-release metrics, staged rollouts and fix verification.

questions.question: Design the client side of a chat app that remains usable on flaky networks: message sending, ordering, deduplication and sync.
questions.model_answer: Use a local database (SQLite/Room/Core Data) as the source of truth that the UI observes. Sending writes the message locally with a client-generated id and `pending` state, and an outbox worker sends it with retries and exponential backoff, marking `sent` when the server acknowledges. The server dedupes by client id, so retries are idempotent. For ordering, rely on server-assigned sequence numbers per conversation and show optimistic local messages in a provisional position until acknowledged. Keep a WebSocket for live events with heartbeats and auto-reconnect, and on reconnect fetch missed messages since the last sequence number, falling back to push notifications and background sync. Handle app death by persisting the outbox, add attachment uploads as resumable jobs, and surface per-message status (sending, failed with retry). Test with network link conditioners and chaos tools.
questions.explanation: Look for local-first design, idempotent sends with client ids, server sequence numbers and reconnect/catch-up logic.

questions.question: Why are you leaving your current job (or why did you leave your last one)?
questions.model_answer: Keep it forward-looking and professional. Situation: 'I have spent two years building internal tools and learned a lot, but the team has stopped investing in new products, so my growth has plateaued.' Task: I want to work on customer-facing systems at larger scale and deepen my backend skills. Action: I proactively asked for stretch work, took on an on-call rotation and a migration project, and confirmed with my manager that the path I want is not available in the near term. Result: I leave on good terms with documentation handed over, and this role matches what I am looking for because of its scale and engineering culture. I never criticize my former employer or colleagues.
questions.explanation: Interviewers screen for negativity, blame and mismatched motivation. A calm, specific, growth-oriented answer without badmouthing wins.

questions.question: Describe your ideal work environment and the kind of manager you work best with.
questions.model_answer: Be honest but flexible, and tie it to results. I do my best work in a team with clear goals, autonomy over how to reach them, and a culture of written communication and code review. I like a manager who sets context and priorities, gives frequent specific feedback and is available when I am blocked, but doesn't micromanage. Situation example: at my last company, weekly 1:1s with clear expectations helped me raise a delayed project's delivery rate; my action was to bring a short agenda and risks each week; the result was fewer surprises and an on-time release. I adapt to other styles too, for example by asking for more check-ins when a manager prefers hands-on involvement.
questions.explanation: Look for self-awareness plus adaptability. Avoid describing an environment so narrow that the company could not offer it.

questions.question: Tell me about the project you are most proud of.
questions.model_answer: Choose a project with measurable impact and your clear personal contribution. Situation: our checkout page had a 9-second load time and conversion was falling. Task: I owned the performance improvement as the lead frontend developer. Action: I profiled with Lighthouse and found oversized images, a blocking third-party script and an N+1 API call; I introduced lazy loading, moved the script to async, batched the request and added a performance budget in CI. I also documented the findings for the team. Result: load time dropped to 2.5 seconds, conversion rose 11%, and the budget prevented regressions afterwards. I am proud of it because it combined measurement, teamwork and lasting process change.
questions.explanation: Use specifics: numbers, your role versus the team's, and what you learned. Avoid vague 'we did great things'.

questions.question: What motivates you at work?
questions.model_answer: Name genuine motivators and back them with an example. I am motivated by solving real user problems and by seeing the effect of my work in measurable outcomes. Situation: support tickets about a confusing export feature kept growing. Task: nobody owned it, but I wanted to fix the root cause. Action: I sat in on support calls for a morning, redesigned the flow with a designer and shipped a simplified version in two sprints. Result: related tickets fell by 60% and I received direct customer thanks. I am also motivated by learning from stronger engineers and by mentoring, so I look for teams that value both.
questions.explanation: Authenticity matters; answers should align with the role (for example impact, craft, learning) and avoid 'only money' or generic buzzwords.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to juggle several high-priority tasks at once. How did you decide what to do first?
questions.model_answer: Situation: in one week I had a production bug affecting a few customers, a feature demo for a prospective client and a code review blocking a teammate. Task: deliver all without dropping quality. Action: I listed the three items with impact and deadline, flagged the conflict to my manager and agreed the priorities: the production bug first because it was affecting revenue, the review next because it took 20 minutes and unblocked someone, then the demo preparation. I communicated expected times to each stakeholder and asked a colleague to help with demo data. Result: the bug was fixed in two hours, the teammate was unblocked the same day and the demo went well. Lesson: prioritize by impact and urgency, communicate early and delegate when possible.
questions.explanation: Look for an explicit prioritization framework, proactive communication to stakeholders and a concrete result.

questions.question: Describe a time you went above and beyond what was asked.
questions.model_answer: Situation: a client asked me to add a CSV export button. Task: deliver exactly that by Friday. Action: while implementing it I noticed exports of large accounts timed out and users would assume the feature was broken. After finishing the requested scope, I spent extra time moving the export to a background job with an email link, added a progress message and wrote a short usage note, and I told my manager and the client why I did it. Result: the feature worked for the biggest customers, support tickets about exports never appeared, and the client requested the same pattern for other reports. I made sure the extra work didn't delay the agreed deliverable or hide scope changes.
questions.explanation: Going beyond must be useful and transparent. Beware answers that show scope creep or unsustainable overwork.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new technology quickly to deliver a project.
questions.model_answer: Situation: our team inherited a service written in Go, and I only knew Python and JavaScript. Task: fix a critical bug and add an endpoint within two weeks.
